claim: Layer 1 (L1) receives massive cortico-cortical, commissural and associational projections.
source: Layer (L)1, beside receiving massive cortico-cortical, commissural and associational projections, is the termination zone of tufted dendrites of pyramidal neurons and the area of Ca2+ spike initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about L1 anatomy.

claim: Layer 1 is the termination zone of tufted dendrites of pyramidal neurons.
source: Layer (L)1, beside receiving massive cortico-cortical, commissural and associational projections, is the termination zone of tufted dendrites of pyramidal neurons and the area of Ca2+ spike initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established anatomical feature.

claim: Layer 1 is the area of Ca2+ spike initiation.
source: Layer (L)1, beside receiving massive cortico-cortical, commissural and associational projections, is the termination zone of tufted dendrites of pyramidal neurons and the area of Ca2+ spike initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a functional property of L1.

claim: The synaptic organization of Layer 1 in humans is not known.
source: However, its synaptic organization in humans is not known.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: Quantitative 3D models of excitatory synaptic boutons in L1 of the human temporal lobe neocortex were generated from neocortical biopsy tissue.
source: Quantitative 3D models of excitatory synaptic boutons (SBs) in L1 of the human temporal lobe neocortex were generated from neocortical biopsy tissue using transmission electron microscopy, 3D-volume reconstructions, and TEM tomography.
evidence: This describes the primary methodology and data generation of the study.

claim: The majority of excitatory SBs in L1 contained numerous mitochondria comprising ~7% of the total volume.
source: The majority of excitatory SBs contained numerous mitochondria comprising ~7% of the total volume, had a large macular, non-perforated AZ (~0.20 µm2) and were predominantly located on dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the 3D reconstructions reported in the abstract.

claim: Excitatory SBs in L1 had a large macular, non-perforated active zone of approximately 0.20 µm2.
source: The majority of excitatory SBs contained numerous mitochondria comprising ~7% of the total volume, had a large macular, non-perforated AZ (~0.20 µm2) and were predominantly located on dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study reported in the abstract.

claim: Excitatory SBs in L1 were predominantly located on dendritic spines.
source: The majority of excitatory SBs contained numerous mitochondria comprising ~7% of the total volume, had a large macular, non-perforated AZ (~0.20 µm2) and were predominantly located on dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Excitatory SBs in L1 had a total pool of approximately 3500 synaptic vesicles.
source: Excitatory SBs had a total pool of ~3500 SVs, a relatively large readily releasable (~4 SVs), recycling (~470 SVs) and resting (~2900 SVs) pool.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from vesicle counting reported in the abstract.

claim: Excitatory SBs in L1 had a readily releasable pool of approximately 4 synaptic vesicles.
source: Excitatory SBs had a total pool of ~3500 SVs, a relatively large readily releasable (~4 SVs), recycling (~470 SVs) and resting (~2900 SVs) pool.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from vesicle pool analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Excitatory SBs in L1 had a recycling pool of approximately 470 synaptic vesicles.
source: Excitatory SBs had a total pool of ~3500 SVs, a relatively large readily releasable (~4 SVs), recycling (~470 SVs) and resting (~2900 SVs) pool.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from vesicle pool analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Excitatory SBs in L1 had a resting pool of approximately 2900 synaptic vesicles.
source: Excitatory SBs had a total pool of ~3500 SVs, a relatively large readily releasable (~4 SVs), recycling (~470 SVs) and resting (~2900 SVs) pool.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from vesicle pool analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Astrocytic coverage of excitatory SBs suggests both synaptic crosstalk or removal of spilled glutamate by astrocytic processes at synaptic complexes.
source: Astrocytic coverage of excitatory SBs suggests both synaptic crosstalk or removal of spilled glutamate by astrocytic processes at synaptic complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the astrocytic coverage findings presented in the abstract.

claim: The mammalian neocortex comprises over 75% of the gray matter.
source: The mammalian neocortex is the most complex part of the brain comprising over 75% of the gray matter.
evidence: This is stated as an established anatomical fact in the introduction.

claim: The neocortex is organized into distinct layers with different networks of neurons.
source: One fundamental feature established during development is the formation of distinct layers with different networks of neurons and its organization into vertically oriented slabs, so-called cortical columns (Marin-Padilla, 1978; reviewed by Rockland and DeFelipe, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as an established feature of neocortical organization.

claim: The neocortex is organized into vertically oriented slabs called cortical columns.
source: One fundamental feature established during development is the formation of distinct layers with different networks of neurons and its organization into vertically oriented slabs, so-called cortical columns (Marin-Padilla, 1978; reviewed by Rockland and DeFelipe, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as an established feature of neocortical organization.

claim: Cortical layers are established in an 'inside layers first-outside layers last' fashion.
source: This organization is established in an 'inside layers first-outside layers last' fashion (Luskin and Shatz, 1985a, Luskin and Shatz, 1985b; reviewed by Cooper, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published literature describing cortical development.

claim: Layer 1 is generated first, originating from the marginal zone, as an exception to the inside-first pattern.
source: The exception, besides layer (L)6, is L1 generated first originating from the marginal zone (Marín-Padilla, 1998; reviewed by Bystron et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published literature describing the developmental origin of L1.

claim: Layer 1 is highly conserved across cortical areas and higher mammalian species.
source: Remarkably, L1 is highly conserved across cortical areas and higher mammalian species, but its importance was long underestimated.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation about L1 across species.

claim: Layer 1 is now considered the predominant input layer for top-down information.
source: However, L1 is now considered the predominant input layer for top-down information, relayed by a rich, dense network of cortico-cortical, cortico-thalamic, commissural, and associational long-range axonal projections.
evidence: This is stated as current understanding of L1 function in the introduction.

claim: In humans, Layer 1 contains both excitatory Cajal-Retzius cells and a heterogeneous population of inhibitory neurons.
source: In humans, and thus different from experimental animals, both L1 excitatory Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells (Anstötz et al., 2014) and a quite heterogeneous population of inhibitory neurons (see for example Jiang et al., 2013; Boldog et al., 2018; Obermayer et al., 2018; Kwon et al., 2019; reviewed by Huang et al., 2024) provide signals to the terminal tuft dendrites of pyramidal neurons of the underlying cortical layers.
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies describing the cellular composition of human L1.

claim: Layer 1 is a central locus of neocortical associations controlled by distinct types of inhibition and feedforward excitation.
source: Thus, L1 is a central locus of neocortical associations controlled by distinct types of inhibition and feedforward excitation (Schuman et al., 2019; Hartung and Letzkus, 2021, reviewed by Schuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from recent reviews describing the functional role of L1.

claim: The temporal lobe neocortex encompasses approximately 20% of the entire cerebral cortex in humans.
source: Notably, in humans, the TLN encompasses approximately 20% of the entire cerebral cortex (Kiernan, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as a quantitative anatomical fact.

claim: The human temporal lobe neocortex is recognized as a highly specialized associative neocortex with homotypic granular six-layered organization.
source: It is recognized as a highly specialized associative neocortex, characterized by its homotypic granular six-layered organization (von Economo and Koskinas, 1925; Palomero-Gallagher and Zilles, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from published literature describing the structural organization of the temporal lobe.

claim: The human temporal lobe neocortex plays a crucial role in auditory, visual, vestibular, linguistic, and olfactory processing.
source: The human TLN plays a crucial role in various cognitive functions, including auditory, visual, vestibular, linguistic, and olfactory processing.
evidence: This is stated as an established functional property of the temporal lobe.

claim: The human temporal lobe neocortex serves as the epicenter and onset site for temporal lobe epilepsy.
source: Lastly, the human TLN serves as the epicenter and onset site for temporal lobe epilepsy (Allone et al., 2017; Tai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as a clinical characteristic of the temporal lobe.

claim: Detailed and quantitative descriptions of synaptic complexes in L1 of the human brain are to date non-existent.
source: Nevertheless, detailed and quantitative descriptions of synaptic complexes in L1 of the human brain are to date non-existent.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the current study.

claim: Layer 1 in the adult mammalian neocortex can be subdivided into two sublaminae, L1a and L1b.
source: L1 in the adult mammalian neocortex represents a relatively cell sparse layer, that in humans can be subdivided into two sublaminae, L1a and L1b, as revealed in semithin sections (Figure 1A) and Golgi-preparations (Figure 1B, C, F and G), as well as at the TEM level (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple imaging modalities shown in Figure 1.

claim: L1a is more dominated by a dense network of astrocytes of different shape and size.
source: L1a is more dominated by a dense network of astrocytes of different shape and size, their fine processes (Figure 2A), the occurrence of reactive microglia (Figures 1H, I, 2A) and terminal tuft dendrites of pyramidal neurons throughout the neuropil of L1 (Figures 1H, I, 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the TEM images shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Lipofuscin granules were frequently noted in astrocytes, reactive microglia, and L1 neurons.
source: Lipofuscin granules, indicative of aging, were frequently noted in astrocytes, reactive microglia (Figure 2A), and L1 neurons, although their abundance, size, and morphology varied considerably.
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy images, particularly Figure 2A.

claim: A persistent subpopulation of excitatory Cajal-Retzius cells was found in humans, in contrast to rodents.
source: Remarkably, and in contrast to rodents, a persistent subpopulation of excitatory CR-cells was found in humans, identifiable by the horizontal bipolar orientation with intralaminar long-range horizontal axonal collaterals with a transcolumnar projection (Figure 1E–H; Retzius, 1893; Retzius, 1894; Anstötz et al., 2014; reviewed by Martínez-Cerdeño and Noctor, 2014).
evidence: This is observed in the Golgi preparations shown in Figure 1 and cited from literature.

claim: GABAergic interneurons constitute the predominant class of neurons in L1 of the human temporal lobe neocortex.
source: In the human TLN, GABAergic interneurons constitute the predominant class of neurons in L1, exhibiting significant structural and functional heterogeneity (Figure 1D and E; see also Jiang et al., 2013; Verhoog et al., 2016; Boldog et al., 2018; Obermayer et al., 2018; Kwon et al., 2019; Schuman et al., 2019, reviewed by Huang et al., 2024) which were found throughout both sublaminae and were sometimes organized in clusters of three to six neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the study and cited from multiple published sources.

claim: The majority of synaptic complexes in L1 were axo-spinous at approximately 80%.
source: The majority of synaptic complexes in L1 were axo-spinous (~80%, Figure 2B, D and E), the remainder were axo-dendritic, some of which but not all were regarded as putative GABAergic terminals (Figure 2C; but see Silver et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: A total of 361 synaptic boutons was completely reconstructed from four patients in six series.
source: To achieve this, a total of 361 SBs was completely reconstructed out of four patients in six series containing 100–150 ultrathin sections/series.
evidence: This describes the sample size and methodology of the study.

claim: A total of 190 SBs and 184 AZs were reconstructed in L1a.
source: A total of 190 SBs and 184 AZs (L1a) and 171 SBs and 165 AZs (L1b) using neocortical access tissue (see Material and Methods; Source data 2) were completely 3D-reconstructed and quantified using fine-scale TEM, digital TEM images, and subsequent 3D-volume reconstructions.
evidence: This describes the sample size for L1a in the study.

claim: A total of 171 SBs and 165 AZs were reconstructed in L1b.
source: A total of 190 SBs and 184 AZs (L1a) and 171 SBs and 165 AZs (L1b) using neocortical access tissue (see Material and Methods; Source data 2) were completely 3D-reconstructed and quantified using fine-scale TEM, digital TEM images, and subsequent 3D-volume reconstructions.
evidence: This describes the sample size for L1b in the study.

claim: Approximately 81% of SBs in L1a were found on dendritic spines.
source: In both sublaminae, SBs were predominantly found on dendritic spines (~81%; L1a) and ~79% (L1b), the remainder were located on dendritic shafts.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the structural analysis.

claim: Approximately 79% of SBs in L1b were found on dendritic spines.
source: In both sublaminae, SBs were predominantly found on dendritic spines (~81%; L1a) and ~79% (L1b), the remainder were located on dendritic shafts.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The majority of SBs on spines in L1a were located on mushroom spines at approximately 83%.
source: The majority of SBs on spines were located on mushroom spines (L1a: ~83%, L1b: ~73%), a smaller fraction on stubby spines (L1a: ~11%, L1b: ~9%) or on thin elongated spines (L1a: 6%, L1b: ~22%; Figure 2E), the remainder were not classifiable.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from spine type classification.

claim: The majority of SBs on spines in L1b were located on mushroom spines at approximately 73%.
source: The majority of SBs on spines were located on mushroom spines (L1a: ~83%, L1b: ~73%), a smaller fraction on stubby spines (L1a: ~11%, L1b: ~9%) or on thin elongated spines (L1a: 6%, L1b: ~22%; Figure 2E), the remainder were not classifiable.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from spine type classification.

claim: Approximately 90% of spines in L1a and L1b contained a spine apparatus.
source: Remarkably, ~90% of spines in L1a and L1b contained a spine apparatus (Figure 2E), a specialized derivate from the endoplasmic reticulum, structures that increase spine motility and may also stabilize the synaptic complex during signal transduction (Deller et al., 2003; reviewed by Knott and Holtmaat, 2008).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1 was 5.26*10^8±8.44*10^7 synapses/mm3.
source: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1 was relatively high with a value of 5.26*108±8.44*107, 5.52*108±1.25*108 synapses/mm3 in L1a and 5.01*108±1.40*107 synapses/mm3 in L1b, ranging from 4.08*108–6.31*108 (L1a) and from 4.87*108–5.15*108 (L1b), respectively (Supplementary file 1; Source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from stereological analysis.

claim: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1a was 5.52*10^8±1.25*10^8 synapses/mm3.
source: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1 was relatively high with a value of 5.26*108±8.44*107, 5.52*108±1.25*108 synapses/mm3 in L1a and 5.01*108±1.40*107 synapses/mm3 in L1b, ranging from 4.08*108–6.31*108 (L1a) and from 4.87*108–5.15*108 (L1b), respectively (Supplementary file 1; Source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from stereological analysis.

claim: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1b was 5.01*10^8±1.40*10^7 synapses/mm3.
source: The average density of synaptic complexes in L1 was relatively high with a value of 5.26*108±8.44*107, 5.52*108±1.25*108 synapses/mm3 in L1a and 5.01*108±1.40*107 synapses/mm3 in L1b, ranging from 4.08*108–6.31*108 (L1a) and from 4.87*108–5.15*108 (L1b), respectively (Supplementary file 1; Source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from stereological analysis.

claim: L1 SBs were on average medium-sized, with a mean surface area of 5.48±1.40 µm2.
source: Overall, L1 SBs were on average medium-sized, with a mean surface area of 5.48±1.40 µm2, and a mean volume of 0.50±0.19 µm3, with a slight difference in size between L1a and L1b.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: L1 SBs had a mean volume of 0.50±0.19 µm3.
source: Overall, L1 SBs were on average medium-sized, with a mean surface area of 5.48±1.40 µm2, and a mean volume of 0.50±0.19 µm3, with a slight difference in size between L1a and L1b.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: SBs in L1 were comparable in size with SBs in L5 and L6, but approximately 2-fold larger than those in L4 of the human temporal lobe neocortex.
source: SBs in L1 were comparable in size with SBs in L5 and L6, but ~2-fold larger than those in L4 of the human TLN (p≤0.001; see also Yakoubi et al., 2019a; Yakoubi et al., 2019b; Schmuhl-Giesen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis with previously published data from other layers.

claim: Mitochondria in L1a had a volume of 0.04±0.02 µm3.
source: When present, mitochondria had a volume of 0.04±0.02 µm3 in L1a and 0.05±0.01 µm3 in L1b, respectively (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: Mitochondria in L1b had a volume of 0.05±0.01 µm3.
source: When present, mitochondria had a volume of 0.04±0.02 µm3 in L1a and 0.05±0.01 µm3 in L1b, respectively (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: Mitochondria contributed approximately 7% to the total bouton volume of SBs in L1.
source: Mitochondria contributed with ~7% (L1) to the total bouton volume of SBs, similar to values in L6 (~6%; Schmuhl-Giesen et al., 2022), but with a ~1.5-fold lower percentage than those in L5 (~12%; Yakoubi et al., 2019a) and L4 (~13%; Yakoubi et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions with comparison to other layers.

claim: A good correlation between the volume of the SBs and that of mitochondria was found for L1a (R2: 0.7528).
source: A good correlation between the volume of the SBs and that of mitochondria was found for L1a (R2: 0.7528; Figure 4B) and for L1b (R2: 0.5992; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A good correlation between the volume of the SBs and that of mitochondria was found for L1b (R2: 0.5992).
source: A good correlation between the volume of the SBs and that of mitochondria was found for L1a (R2: 0.7528; Figure 4B) and for L1b (R2: 0.5992; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The majority (~98%) of SBs in L1a and L1b had only a single active zone.
source: The majority (~98%) of SBs in L1a and L1b had only a single (Figures 2C-E and 3A-C, E) at most two or three AZs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the structural analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PreAZs in L1a were on average 0.18±0.08 µm2 in surface area.
source: On average, PreAZs were 0.18±0.08 µm2 in surface area in L1a and 0.22±0.04 µm2 in L1b with only a slight variability between both sublaminae.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: PreAZs in L1b were on average 0.22±0.04 µm2 in surface area.
source: On average, PreAZs were 0.18±0.08 µm2 in surface area in L1a and 0.22±0.04 µm2 in L1b with only a slight variability between both sublaminae.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: The surface area of PSDs in L1a was 0.21±0.01 µm2.
source: The surface area of PSDs was quite similar to that of PreAZs, 0.21±0.01 µm2 in L1a and 0.22±0.05 µm2 in L1b, respectively (Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: The surface area of PSDs in L1b was 0.22±0.05 µm2.
source: The surface area of PSDs was quite similar to that of PreAZs, 0.21±0.01 µm2 in L1a and 0.22±0.05 µm2 in L1b, respectively (Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions reported in Table 1.

claim: The majority of AZs in L1 (~80%) were of the macular and non-perforated type.
source: Two types of AZs were found: the majority in L1 (~80%) were of the macular and non-perforated type (Figure 3D), the remainder being either horseshoe-shaped or ring-like and perforated (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the structural classification shown in Figure 3.

claim: Only a weak correlation between the surface area of SBs and that of PreAZs was found for L1a and L1b SBs.
source: Notably, our analysis revealed only a weak correlation between the surface area of SBs and that of PreAZs for L1a and L1b SBs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SVs in L1 had an average diameter of 25.03±5.27 nm.
source: Small clear SVs with an average diameter of 25.03±5.27 nm ranging up to ~40 nm (Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from TEM images reported in Table 1.

claim: Using TEM tomography, the SV diameter was on average 30.29±4.67 nm.
source: Using TEM tomography, the SV diameter was on average 30.29±4.67 nm ranging up to ~47 nm (n=38 SBs with a total of 5.834 SVs; Table 1; Source data 3, sheet 05).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from TEM tomography reported in Table 1.

claim: DCVs had an average diameter of 57.97±6.45 nm with no significant difference between L1a and L1b.
source: DCVs (Dense Core Vesicles; Figure 3B, C, E; Source data 2, sheet 01) with an average diameter of 57.97±6.45 nm with no significant difference between both sublaminae.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from TEM images shown in Figure 3.

claim: The total pool of SVs in L1a was on average 2958.62±1940.51.
source: On average, the total pool of SVs was 2958.62±1940.51 in L1a vs. 3903.32±1852.23 in L1b with an average of 3430.97±1773.77 for L1 (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from vesicle counting reported in Table 1.

claim: The total pool of SVs in L1b was on average 3903.32±1852.23.
source: On average, the total pool of SVs was 2958.62±1940.51 in L1a vs. 3903.32±1852.23 in L1b with an average of 3430.97±1773.77 for L1 (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from vesicle counting reported in Table 1.

claim: The total pool in L1b was significantly larger (p≤0.01) by approximately 1.3-fold when compared to L1a.
source: Remarkably, the total pool in L1b was significantly larger (p≤0.01) by ~1.3-fold when compared to L1a.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between the two sublaminae.

claim: SVs contributed with approximately 5% (0.03 µm3) in L1a to the total volume of SBs.
source: SVs contributed with ~5% (0.03 µm3) in L1a and ~4% (0.02 µm3) in L1b to the total volume of SBs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions.

claim: SVs contributed with approximately 4% (0.02 µm3) in L1b to the total volume of SBs.
source: SVs contributed with ~5% (0.03 µm3) in L1a and ~4% (0.02 µm3) in L1b to the total volume of SBs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from 3D reconstructions.

claim: The average number of SVs in the putative RRP/PreAZ for L1 was 3.60±4.24 SVs at p10 nm.
source: The average number of SVs in the putative RRP/PreAZ for L1 was 3.60±4.24 SVs at p10 nm (L1a: 5.90±5.05 SVs and L1b: 1.29±1.87 SVs) with a significant difference (p≤0.01) by ~4.5-fold between the two sublaminae (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RRP/PreAZ at p10 nm in L1a was 5.90±5.05 SVs.
source: The average number of SVs in the putative RRP/PreAZ for L1 was 3.60±4.24 SVs at p10 nm (L1a: 5.90±5.05 SVs and L1b: 1.29±1.87 SVs) with a significant difference (p≤0.01) by ~4.5-fold between the two sublaminae (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RRP/PreAZ at p10 nm in L1b was 1.29±1.87 SVs.
source: The average number of SVs in the putative RRP/PreAZ for L1 was 3.60±4.24 SVs at p10 nm (L1a: 5.90±5.05 SVs and L1b: 1.29±1.87 SVs) with a significant difference (p≤0.01) by ~4.5-fold between the two sublaminae (Table 1; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RRP/PreAZ at the p20 nm criterion was on average 19.05±17.23 SVs.
source: The putative RRP/PreAZ at the p20 nm criterion was on average 19.05±17.23 SVs (L1a: 25.04±21.09 SVs and L1b: 13.07±13.87 SVs) and thus nearly 2-fold larger for L1a, although with a huge variability, but even though it may point to sublaminae-specific differences in Pr, synaptic efficacy, strength, and paired-pulse behavior at individual SBs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RRP/PreAZ at p20 nm in L1a was 25.04±21.09 SVs.
source: The putative RRP/PreAZ at the p20 nm criterion was on average 19.05±17.23 SVs (L1a: 25.04±21.09 SVs and L1b: 13.07±13.87 SVs) and thus nearly 2-fold larger for L1a, although with a huge variability, but even though it may point to sublaminae-specific differences in Pr, synaptic efficacy, strength, and paired-pulse behavior at individual SBs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RRP/PreAZ at p20 nm in L1b was 13.07±13.87 SVs.
source: The putative RRP/PreAZ at the p20 nm criterion was on average 19.05±17.23 SVs (L1a: 25.04±21.09 SVs and L1b: 13.07±13.87 SVs) and thus nearly 2-fold larger for L1a, although with a huge variability, but even though it may point to sublaminae-specific differences in Pr, synaptic efficacy, strength, and paired-pulse behavior at individual SBs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RP/PreAZ at the 60–200 nm perimeter criterion was 390.12±286.89 SVs in L1a.
source: The putative RP/PreAZ at the 60–200 nm perimeter criterion was 390.12±286.89 SVs in L1a and 535.88±321.16 in L1b with no significant difference between both sublaminae (Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative RP/PreAZ at the 60–200 nm perimeter criterion was 535.88±321.16 SVs in L1b.
source: The putative RP/PreAZ at the 60–200 nm perimeter criterion was 390.12±286.89 SVs in L1a and 535.88±321.16 in L1b with no significant difference between both sublaminae (Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative resting pool of SVs contained on average 2515.02±1588.99 SVs in L1a.
source: The putative resting pool of SVs contained on average 2515.02±1588.99 SVs in L1a and 3277.97±1480.96 SVs in L1b with a significant difference between the two sublaminae (p≤0.01, Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The putative resting pool of SVs contained on average 3277.97±1480.96 SVs in L1b.
source: The putative resting pool of SVs contained on average 2515.02±1588.99 SVs in L1a and 3277.97±1480.96 SVs in L1b with a significant difference between the two sublaminae (p≤0.01, Table 1; Source data 2, sheet 01).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from perimeter analysis reported in Table 1.

claim: The number of SVs in the putative resting pool in L1b was about 1.3-fold larger when compared to L1a.
source: The number of SVs in the putative resting pool in L1b was about 1.3-fold larger when compared to L1a.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis between the two sublaminae.

claim: In the majority of PreAZs (~98%), more than 2 docked SVs were observed, with the most being 8 in L1a and 6 in L1b.
source: Second, the majority of PreAZs (~98%) contained more than 2, the most 8 (L1a) and 6 (L1b) 'docked' SVs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from TEM tomography analysis.

claim: On average, 3.71±1.38 docked SVs were found at individual PreAZs in L1a.
source: On average, 3.71±1.38 'docked' SVs (L1a) and 3.42±1.34 'docked SVs' (L1b) were found at individual PreAZs with similar values for both sublaminae.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from TEM tomography reported in Table 2.

claim: On average, 3.42±1.34 docked SVs were found at individual PreAZs in L1b.
source: On average, 3.71±1.38 'docked' SVs (L1a) and 3.42±1.34 'docked SVs' (L1b) were found at individual PreAZs with similar values for both sublaminae.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from TEM tomography reported in Table 2.

claim: Astrocytic processes in L1 contributed by approximately 20% to the total volume of the human temporal lobe neocortex.
source: Astrocytic processes in L1 contributed by ~20% to the total volume of the human TLN, which is similar to findings in L6 of the human TLN.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from volumetric analysis shown in Figure 6C and Table 3.

claim: The highest degree (~70–80%) of astrocytic processes was measured in L4.
source: The highest degree (~70%) of astrocytic processes was measured in L4 (Figure 6C; Source data 4, sheet 01, Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from volumetric analysis shown in Figure 6C and Table 3.

claim: In L1, the majority of spine and shaft synapses were not (~70%) or only partially (~20%) covered by fine astrocytic processes.
source: A second, more detailed measurement (Figure 6D, Table 3; Source data 4, sheet 02), in which the percentage of AZs covered by astrocytes was analyzed, demonstrated that (1) in L1, the majority of spine and shaft synapses were not (~70%) or only partially (~20%) covered. by fine astrocytic processes
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from astrocytic coverage analysis shown in Figure 6D and Table 3.

claim: Only in a small proportion (~10%) at both spine and shaft synapses in L1 were fine astrocytic processes forming a 'tripartite' synapse observed.
source: (2) only in a small proportion (~10%) at both spine and shaft synapses fine astrocytic processes forming a 'tripartite' synapse physically isolating the synaptic complexes from the surrounding neuropil were observed
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from astrocytic coverage analysis shown in Figure 6D and Table 3.

claim: In L4, a much higher number of 'tripartite' synaptic complexes (spines: ~50%; shafts: ~20%) was found compared to L1.
source: In L4, a much higher number of 'tripartite' synaptic complexes (spines: ~50%; shafts: ~20%) was found.
evidence: This is a comparative finding between L1 and L4 from astrocytic coverage analysis.

claim: L1 exhibited a relatively high density of synaptic complexes, indicating a relatively robust and thus strong connectivity of neurons within L1 of the human temporal lobe neocortex.
source: Therefore, L1 exhibited a relatively high density of synaptic complexes, indicating a relatively robust and thus strong connectivity of neurons within L1 of the human TLN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the synaptic density measurements.

claim: The quantitative 3D models of the analyzed excitatory SBs showed significant layer-specific differences in structural and synaptic parameters compared to other previously studied layers.
source: In addition to similarities, the quantitative 3D models of the analyzed excitatory SBs showed significant layer-specific differences in structural and synaptic parameters, in particular in the size of AZs and the total pool of SVs, the putative RRP, RP, and resting pool compared to other previously studied layers (Yakoubi et al., 2019a; Yakoubi et al., 2019b; Schmuhl-Giesen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the Discussion.

claim: The low degree of astrocytic coverage of L1 SBs suggests that glutamate spillover, and as a consequence, synaptic cross talk may occur at most synaptic complexes in L1.
source: The low degree of astrocytic coverage of L1 SBs suggests that glutamate spillover, and as a consequence, synaptic cross talk may occur at most synaptic complexes in L1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the astrocytic coverage findings in the Discussion.

claim: The highest synaptic density was observed in L1, indicating a relatively high level of connectivity and synaptic interaction.
source: In summary, the highest synaptic density was observed in L1, indicating a relatively high level of connectivity and synaptic interaction.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the synaptic density findings in the Discussion.

claim: The size of the active zone is one key structural determinant in synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: The number, size, and shape of the AZ, composed of the PreAZ and PSD, is one key structural determinant in synaptic transmission and plasticity (Südhof, 2002; Matz et al., 2010; Holderith et al., 2012) as it represents the docking area of SVs (PreAZs) and the receiving area of neurotransmitter quanta at the PSD (Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as an established principle.

claim: The surface area of AZs in L1 SBs of the human temporal lobe neocortex was on average approximately 0.20 μm2.
source: The surface area of AZs in L1 SBs of the human TLN was on average ∼0.20 μm2.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative findings in the Discussion.

claim: AZs in L1 were approximately 2- to 3-fold larger than those in mouse and non-human primates visual, motor, and somatosensory neocortex.
source: However, they were ∼2- to 3-fold larger than those in mouse and non-human primates visual, motor, and somatosensory neocortex (Bopp et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017) but remarkably even larger than AZs in comparably large CNS terminals like the hippocampal mossy fiber bouton (Rollenhagen et al., 2007), the cerebellar mossy fiber bouton (Xu-Friedman and Regehr, 2003), and the Calyx of Held in the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (Sätzler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis with published data from other species and brain regions.

claim: The comparably large size of the AZs in the human temporal lobe neocortex suggests a larger 'docking' area allowing the fusion of more SVs and thus a larger probability of release.
source: However, the comparably large size of the AZs in the human TLN also suggests a larger 'docking' area allowing the fusion of more SVs and thus a larger Pr.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AZ size findings in the Discussion.

claim: L1-SBs had a total pool size of approximately 3500 SVs/AZ, larger than in other layers of the human temporal lobe neocortex.
source: L1-SBs had a total pool size of ~3500 SVs/AZ, larger than in other layers of the human TLN: ~2-fold in L4 (~1800 SVs; Yakoubi et al., 2019b), ~2.6-fold in L5 (~1350 SVs; Yakoubi et al., 2019a), and ~3-fold in L6 (~1150 SVs; Schmuhl-Giesen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis with published data from other layers.

claim: The putative RRP at L1 PreAZs was on average approximately 4 SVs/AZ for the p10 nm RRP.
source: The putative RRP at L1 PreAZs was on average ~4 SVs/AZ for the p10 nm RRP and similar to that in L5 (~5 SVs/AZ), but significantly smaller by ~5.3-fold to that of L4 (~20 SVs/AZ) and by ~3.5-fold when compared to L6 in the human TLN.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis with other layers in the Discussion.

claim: The size of the putative RP/PreAZ was approximately 470 SVs in human L1 SBs.
source: The size of the putative RP/PreAZ was ∼470 SVs in human L1 SBs and thus ~3-fold larger than that in L6 SBs, ~1.3-fold larger than in L4, and ~2.4-fold larger than in L5 SBs of the human TLN.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis with other layers in the Discussion.

claim: The putative resting pool of SVs at L1 PreAZs in the human temporal lobe neocortex is relatively large at approximately 3000 SVs.
source: Finally, the putative resting pool of SVs at L1 PreAZs in the human TLN is also relatively large (~3000 SVs) and again the largest when compared with other layers in the human TLN (L4 and L5: ~1250 SVs; L6: ~900 SVs).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis with other layers in the Discussion.

claim: Mitochondria play a pivotal role in the recruitment and mobilization of SVs from the RP and resting pool and in the priming and docking process of SVs.
source: Mitochondria play a pivotal role in the recruitment and mobilization of SVs from the RP and resting pool and in the priming and docking process of SVs (Verstreken et al., 2005; Perkins et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2016; reviewed by Dallérac et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as an established function of mitochondria.

claim: Astrocytes serve both as a physical barrier to glutamate diffusion and to mediate neurotransmitter uptake via transporters.
source: Astrocytes serve both as a physical barrier to glutamate diffusion and to mediate neurotransmitter uptake via transporters, thereby regulating the spatial and temporal concentration of neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft (Oliet et al., 2004; Min and Nevian, 2012; Pannasch et al., 2014; reviewed by Dallérac et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as an established function of astrocytes.

claim: Significant layer-specific differences exist in the astrocytic coverage of synaptic complexes in the human temporal lobe neocortex.
source: Remarkably, significant layer-specific differences exist in the astrocytic coverage of synaptic complexes in the human TLN.
evidence: This is a summary of the astrocytic coverage findings in the Discussion.

claim: In L4 and L5, approximately 60–80% of the total volumetric fraction was occupied by astrocytic processes.
source: Although in L4 and L5 ~60–80% of the total volumetric fraction was occupied by astrocytic processes and most of AZs in L4 were tightly ensheathed by fine astrocytic processes, in L1 and L6 the volumetric fraction of astrocytic processes was only ~20% with a loose and incomplete coverage of AZs in L1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from volumetric analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In L1 and L6, the volumetric fraction of astrocytic processes was only approximately 20%.
source: Although in L4 and L5 ~60–80% of the total volumetric fraction was occupied by astrocytic processes and most of AZs in L4 were tightly ensheathed by fine astrocytic processes, in L1 and L6 the volumetric fraction of astrocytic processes was only ~20% with a loose and incomplete coverage of AZs in L1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from volumetric analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Layer 1 is the predominant input layer for top-down information, relayed by a rich, dense network of cortico-cortical, commissural, and associational long-range axonal projections.
source: The computational properties of the neocortex depend upon its ability to integrate the information provided by the sensory organs (bottom-up information) with internally generated signals such as expectations or attentional signals (top-down information). This integration occurs at apical tuft dendrites of L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in L1. Importantly, L1 is the predominant input layer for top-down information, relayed by a rich, dense network of cortico-cortical, commissural, and associational long-range axonal projections.
evidence: This is stated as an established functional property of L1 in the Discussion.

claim: In humans, there is a persistent subpopulation of Cajal-Retzius cells that provides excitation due to their long-range transcolumnar axonal projection to the terminal tuft dendrites.
source: In humans, there is a persistent subpopulation of CR-cells that provides excitation due to their long-range transcolumnar axonal projection to the terminal tuft dendrites (Anstötz et al., 2014), but may also control the population of GABAergic interneurons, which is as of date unknown.
evidence: This is cited from published literature and observed in the current study.

claim: Layer 1 of the neocortex is a central locus of neocortical associations controlled by excitation and distinct types of inhibition.
source: Thus, L1 in the human neocortex is a central locus of neocortical associations controlled by excitation and distinct types of inhibition (reviewed by Hartung and Letzkus, 2021; Schuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from recent reviews as an established functional property.

claim: Layer 1 of the neocortex can be regarded as a complex and intricate layer serving different functions including gating inputs, conveying expectations and context, and mediating states of consciousness, attention, cross-modal interactions, sensory perception, and learning.
source: Hence, L1 of the neocortex can be regarded as a complex and intricate layer of the brain serving different functions, for example to gate inputs, convey expectations and context as well as mediate states of consciousness, attention, cross-modal interactions, sensory perception, and learning (Bastos et al., 2012; Heeger, 2017; Zagha, 2020; reviewed by Gilbert and Li, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature as established functional properties of L1.

claim: Layer 1 plays a crucial role in top-down attentional processes, aiding in directing attention based on goals and intentions.
source: Recent studies have revealed that L1 plays a crucial role in top-down attentional processes, aiding in directing attention, based on our goals and intentions (Hartung and Letzkus, 2021; Schuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from recent studies as an established functional property.

claim: Layer 1 is implicated in the formation and consolidation of long-term memories.
source: Additionally, L1 is implicated in the formation and consolidation of long-term memories, with disruptions in L1 function associated with memory deficits.
evidence: This is stated as an established functional property of L1.

claim: Layer 1 contributes to brain plasticity, which involves the brain's ability to change and adapt in response to experience.
source: Furthermore, L1 contributes to brain plasticity, which involves the brain's ability to change and adapt in response to experience, including the process by which synapses alter in strength and number (reviewed by Hartung and Letzkus, 2021; Schuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from reviews as an established functional property.

claim: Human brain tissue sampling during epilepsy surgery was approved by the Ethical Committees of the Rheinische Friedrich-Wilhelms-University/University Hospital Bonn and the University of Bochum.
source: Human brain tissue sampling during epilepsy surgery has been provided by Dr. med. Dorothea Miller, PD Dr. med. Marec von Lehe, Department of Neurosurgery, Knappschaftschafts/Universitäts-Krankenhaus Bochum and were approved by the Ethical Committees of the Rheinische Friedrich-Wilhelms-University/University Hospital Bonn (Ethical votum of the Medical Faculty to Prof. Dr. med. Johannes Schramm and Prof. Dr. rer. nat. Joachim Lübke, Nr. 146/11), the University of Bochum (Ethical votum of the Medical Faculty to PD Dr. med. Marec von Lehe and Prof. Dr. rer. nat. Joachim Lübke, Reg. No. 5190-14-15; and renewed Ethical votum of the Medical Faculty to Dr. med. Dorothea Miller and Prof. Dr. rer. nat. Joachim Lübke, Reg. No. 17–6199-BR).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: All neocortical access tissues were obtained from patients suffering from drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.
source: All neocortical access tissues were obtained from patients suffering from drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy (1 male and 3 female, 24–65 years in age for L1, and additionally 2 male and 3 female, 25–63 in age for L4; see also Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the patient population and tissue source.

claim: In all cases, the circumscribed epileptic focus was in the hippocampus proper, but not in the neocortical access regions of the temporal lobe.
source: In all cases, the circumscribed epileptic focus was in the hippocampus proper, but not in the neocortical access regions of the TL.
evidence: This describes the location of the epileptic focus relative to the tissue samples.

claim: The non-affected non-epileptic neocortical access tissue samples were always taken far from the epileptic focus and may thus be regarded as non-epileptic.
source: The non-affected non-epileptic neocortical access tissue samples were always taken far from the epileptic focus and may thus be regarded as non-epileptic, as also demonstrated by functional studies using the same experimental approach (Mohan et al., 2015; Molnár et al., 2016; Seeman et al., 2018; Obermayer et al., 2018; reviewed by Mansvelder et al., 2019).
evidence: This justifies the use of epilepsy surgery tissue as representative of non-epileptic tissue, citing functional studies.
